title: Drafting a Manuscript
answer: Drafting a manuscript in academic writing covers the preparation of a complete research paper, from outline and first draft through revision before submission. It includes structuring sections such as introduction, methods, results, and discussion, and ensuring that every claim is supported by a source. The AI Researcher's library of 135 research papers and 10,767 extracted claims offers a reference base for checking statements during drafting. The work sits within academic writing and peer review, where clarity, accuracy, and proper citation matter more than stylistic flourish.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Drafting a manuscript typically runs on a standard word processor or a collaborative editor, often paired with a reference manager for citations. AI assistance may be provided through a cloud-based language model accessed by API or a local model running on the researcher's own machine. The site's catalogue of 732 AI tools and 803 scientific models indicates the range of software that can be connected to a drafting workflow, but the core infrastructure remains the document file and the citation database. No special hardware is required beyond a computer with internet access for cloud tools.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done iteratively. A researcher usually begins with an outline, then expands each section with evidence from the literature, and revises for coherence and precision. AI tools can help by summarizing a paper, suggesting alternative phrasing, or flagging a sentence that lacks a supporting citation. On this site, extracted claims are linked to the original paper, so a drafter can verify a statement against its source rather than relying on a secondary search summary. The final step is a careful human read to ensure the manuscript's argument is sound and the voice is the author's own.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in manuscript drafting center on authorship, plagiarism, and the provenance of every factual claim. A researcher must not present AI-generated text as their own without review, and must ensure that paraphrased material does not reproduce wording too closely. This site's practice is to link content to the original paper, never to the Consensus search tool, which keeps the chain of evidence direct and auditable. Risk also includes the possibility that an AI model introduces a plausible but false citation, so every reference must be checked against the actual source before submission.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Drafting assistants are moving toward tighter integration with reference managers and journal submission systems, so that a manuscript can be checked for claim support and formatting as it is written. Future tools may compare a draft against a library of extracted claims and flag unsupported sentences in real time. The site's growing collection of 10,767 claims and 91 AI books suggests a direction where drafting is grounded in a structured, queryable evidence base. The human author will still set the argument and take responsibility, but the mechanical work of checking and formatting will become more automated.
